headline: High-risk workspace overlap: Roo Code’s broad filesystem/MCP/browser defaults can conflict with ms-swift’s file and shell operations, creating leakage and cascading-error risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Roo Code can use MCP, browser, and workspace files by default, so it may ingest attacker-controlled content from shared files or tools. ms-swift reads/writes files and runs shell/Python workflows, so if its outputs are copied into Roo Code, instruction-like content can be misread. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred from overlapping file surfaces.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace or copied artifacts
IF Roo Code parses file or MCP content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Disable MCP for the Roo Code session
Require manual review of any file passed from ms-swift to Roo Code
Prefix imported artifacts as data-only in prompts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Roo Code has broad network egress and handles model provider API keys, while ms-swift handles hub/sdk tokens and writes logs, checkpoints, and training outputs. If they share a workspace, sensitive files can be exposed to Roo Code’s broader outbound paths. The pairwise leakage pathway is plausible in default use and the blast radius includes secrets and work products.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace or log directory
IF Roo Code is configured to send workspace content to a remote model API
mitigations: Move secrets out of shared folders
Use separate OS users or containers
Restrict Roo Code to a scrubbed workspace copy
Rotate any exposed hub/model API tokens
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; Roo Code also modifies git state and uses per-workspace shared state via filesystem. ms-swift can execute shell commands and write files, so concurrent edits to the same repo or workspace can race and corrupt state. Because Roo Code’s defaults are explicitly shared via filesystem, the conflict is credible without extra assumptions.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or git repository
IF Roo Code and ms-swift run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git worktrees or branches per agent
Add a manual lock file before edits
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Roo Code can act on workspace files and git state, while ms-swift can generate logs, configs, and training outputs that Roo Code may treat as authoritative. If ms-swift emits an incorrect artifact, Roo Code can propagate it into code changes or commits without a verification step. The interaction is not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF Roo Code consumes ms-swift outputs as instructions or facts
IF Roo Code is allowed to commit or edit based on those outputs
mitigations: Require human verification before acting on ms-swift outputs
Mark generated artifacts as untrusted
Use a review-only mode for Roo Code
Keep ms-swift outputs in a quarantine folder
requires-engineering: add schema validation for exchanged artifacts

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents touch secrets and files, but the profiles do not show a specific residency or certification mismatch. The main compliance concern is retention and handling of hub/model API tokens, logs, and training outputs across two open-source tools with different default storage patterns. Because no explicit policy gap is documented, this is a moderate risk rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in shared workspace files or logs
IF retention/deletion policies differ between the two operators or deployments
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Set short log retention
Document deletion/export procedures
Review token storage locations
requires-engineering: align retention controls across deployments
